profile.summary: This benchmark asks a method to look at a protein homodimer interface and say whether it is physiological or a crystallographic contact, scoring each entry so that a higher score means more likely physiological. The entries are 1,671 curated homodimer interfaces, 840 physiological and 831 non-physiological, taken from the community-wide study of Schweke and colleagues published in 2023. This package is not the original study: it turns that benchmark into an OpenEBench experiment, with gold-standard labels, four homology-aware five-fold cross-validation splits, the scores of 14 reference methods, validation and scoring scripts, and a static page that scores a submitted CSV in the browser and ranks it against those methods. Anyone with an interface classifier can run it against a published leaderboard without reimplementing the comparison.

summary_quotes.text: Benchmark task: discriminate **physiological** from **crystallographic (non-physiological)** protein homodimer interfaces. 1,671 curated entries (840 physiological, 831 non-physiological).

> **Original work.** The benchmark was published by Schweke H, Xu Q, Tauriello G, *et al.* (2023) *Discriminating physiological from non-physiological interfaces in structures of protein complexes: A community-wide study.* Proteomics 23(17):e2200323, [doi:10.1002/pmic.202200323](https://doi.org/10.1002/pmic.202200323). The data come from the community repository [vibbits/Elixir-3DBioInfo-Benchmark-Protein-Interfaces](https://github.com/vibbits/Elixir-3DBioInfo-Benchmark-Protein-Interfaces). This repository turns the benchmark into an OpenEBench experiment

OpenEBench implementation of the ELIXIR 3D-BioInfo benchmark for discriminating physiological from crystallographic (non-physiological) protein homodimer interfaces: schema-validated OpenEBench metadata (Community, Benchmarking Event, Challenge, Metrics, Tools, Contacts), the datasets of 14 reference scoring methods (13 research groups and a random-forest consensus), the gold-standard labels, four homology-aware cross-validation fold assignments, the benchmark workflow scripts (validation, metric computation, consolidation), and a static web page that evaluates new predictions in the browser and ranks them against the reference methods.

The benchmark has 1,671 entries (840 physiological and 831 non-physiological): the 1,677 entries of the curated annotation of the benchmark authors, without the six entries flagged for deletion. The labels are those of the curated annotation, which differs for 16 entries from the original publication (Schweke et al. 2023, Proteomics 23(17):e2200323, doi:10.1002/pmic.202200323; 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological interfaces).

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a scoring function can tell a biologically real homodimer interface from one that only exists because of crystal packing. A submission is a ranking of the benchmark entries, higher meaning more likely physiological, so the main metrics are threshold-free, and threshold-based metrics are reported alongside. The package's own contribution is comparability: it fixes the labels, the folds and the metric code, so a new method's numbers can be put beside the 14 reference methods rather than computed under its own conventions.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The entries come from the original community study's curated annotation: 1,677 entries less the six flagged for deletion, leaving 1,671, of which 840 are physiological and 831 are not. The Zenodo record states that these labels are the curated annotation and that they differ for 16 entries from the original 2023 publication, which reported 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological interfaces. The reference scores are the ones the 13 research groups submitted to the original benchmark repository, plus a random-forest consensus whose scores are the leave-one-out probabilities provided there. The splits are the package's own work and are documented as such: they are not the folds of the original study. Four strategies are offered, all built so that homologous interfaces stay in one fold, because 1000 of the 1671 entries, 60 per cent, share a CATH superfamily with at least one other entry and a random split would put near-identical interfaces on both sides. Strategy 1 groups by CATH superfamily with a UniProt gene fallback, 853 groups. Strategy 2 clusters chain sequences with MMseqs2 at 25 per cent identity and 50 per cent one-sided coverage, 1076 clusters. Strategy 2b is a BLASTClust clustering at the same nominal parameters, 1045 clusters, which the document calls the most defensible sequence-identity split. Strategy 3, the recommended default and the one the published leaderboard uses, takes the connected components of the union of Strategies 1 and 2b, 688 components with a largest component of 132 entries. All four are verified to have no group spanning more than one fold.

quotes.text: The benchmark has 1,671 entries (840 physiological and 831 non-physiological): the 1,677 entries of the curated annotation of the benchmark authors, without the six entries flagged for deletion. The labels are those of the curated annotation, which differs for 16 entries from the original publication (Schweke et al. 2023, Proteomics 23(17):e2200323, doi:10.1002/pmic.202200323; 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological interfaces).
The scores of the 13 research groups are those submitted to the original benchmark repository; the random-forest consensus uses the leave-one-out probabilities provided there.

**These splits are defined for this package; they are not the folds of Schweke et al.** (Strategies 1 and 3 are grouping rules defined for this package, Strategy 2 is a clustering computed for this package with MMseqs2, and Strategy 2b is the BLASTClust clustering of this benchmark, published in `data/ppi_benchmark_seqs.clust_25_05`.) The manuscript describes a 5-fold cross-validated ROC analysis used to select the best score of each group and its threshold (the point of the ROC most distant from the diagonal; Methods 2.3 and Figure S1 of the supplement). The folds of that analysis are not reproduced here. The splits below keep homologous interfaces together in one fold, and are a proposal of this package.

1000 of 1671 benchmark entries (60%) share a CATH superfamily with at least one other entry. A random split would routinely place near-identical or homologous interfaces in both the training and held-out folds of the same run, inflating any cross-validated performance estimate.

## Strategy 1 -- CATH superfamily / UniProt gene grouping (original proposal) Group key: CATH superfamily (primary), UniProt gene id (fallback when superfamily is missing), singleton (fallback when both are missing). 853 groups, largest group 42 entries.

## Strategy 2 -- Sequence-identity clustering with MMseqs2 (this package's own run) Real pairwise sequence identity, not an annotation proxy. One representative chain sequence was extracted per benchmark entry directly from the PDB structure files in `benchmark_pdb_format/` (BioPython `PPBuilder`, 1677/1677 succeeded, saved as `benchmark_sequences.fasta`), then clustered with: ``` mmseqs easy-cluster benchmark_sequences.fasta clusterRes tmp \ --min-seq-id 0.25 -c 0.5 --cov-mode 1 --cluster-mode 1

blastclust -i sequences.fasta -o clusters.txt -S 25 -L 0.5 -b F`, published at https://biofold.github.io/ppi-benchmark-fair and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/biofold/ppi-benchmark-fair/refs/heads/master/data/ppi_benchmark_seqs.clust_25_05 . **100%% of the file's 1677 entries matched this package's own entry_id convention exactly** (case-insensitive) -- confirming this is the clustering for the identical benchmark, not a different/related dataset. 1045 clusters, largest 27 entries;

## Strategy 3 -- Combined union of Strategy 1 + Strategy 2b (RECOMMENDED) Two entries are forced into the same fold if EITHER signal links them: same CATH superfamily/gene (Strategy 1) OR same blastclust sequence cluster (Strategy 2b), computed as connected components of the union graph. This is the most conservative option against leakage (a structural match some sequence-clustering misses due to low sequence identity at a conserved fold, or vice versa, is still caught), at the cost of coarser groups (688 components, largest 132 entries)
All four give exactly zero groups spanning more than one fold (verified).

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a CSV with one row per entry and a score where higher means more likely physiological. It is then validated and scored. The validation step checks the submitted identifiers against the public reference list and reports how many are missing or unexpected; read in the code, it requires the columns entry_id and raw_score and marks a submission as an error when coverage is not above 0.5. The scoring step computes AUROC, through the Mann-Whitney rank formulation, and AUCPR as average precision, plus accuracy at a threshold, balanced accuracy, F1 and the Matthews correlation coefficient. The threshold matters and the code is explicit about it: a published decision threshold is used when one is passed, and otherwise the script derives the optimal threshold by Youden's J from the same scored population and flags the value as data-driven rather than published. For the cross-validated leaderboard the README states that the thresholds for balanced accuracy, F1 and MCC are learned on the training folds only, and results are reported as a mean and standard deviation over the five folds. A consolidation step turns the per-participant assessments into one leaderboard. The numbers are also reproducible in two ways: the README reports that its demo submission's AUROC computed with the bundle's cross-validation script agrees with the figure the in-browser page produces.

sections.title: Reading the reference table
sections.body: The README's table of the 14 reference methods carries two caveats that change how it should be read, and both are the package's own. First, the top row is not like the others: the random-forest consensus is a trained classifier rather than a single fixed score, its scores are leave-one-out probabilities taken unchanged from the original benchmark repository, and because leave-one-out does not remove homologous entries from the training set its AUROC should be read as an upper estimate relative to the other methods. Second, the methods did not all score the same entries. The n column ranges from 1,123 to 1,671, a method with fewer entries is evaluated on its own subset, and the README points at QSQE, whose AUCPR exceeds its AUROC, as an example of what that does to a value. Beside the current results the repository also keeps analyses computed before a correction, in a superseded folder, for transparency.

quotes.text: **Random-forest consensus.** Unlike the other 13 methods, which are single fixed scores, the consensus is a trained classifier. Its scores are the leave-one-out probabilities provided in the original benchmark repository (`random_forest_analysis/rf_topk221.out`), used unchanged and not retrained within the folds above. Leave-one-out does not remove homologous entries from the training set, so its AUROC should be read as an upper estimate with respect to the other methods.

`n` is the number of benchmark entries each method scored. Methods with fewer than 1,671 entries are evaluated on their own subset, so values are not strictly comparable across rows (the high AUCPR of QSQE, which is above its AUROC, reflects its subset of 1,123 entries).

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Two ways. The quick way is the interactive page, which scores a submitted CSV in the browser, lets the user pick a cross-validation strategy with Strategy 3 as the recommended default, and ranks the result against the 14 reference methods; the README states no file is uploaded anywhere. The local way is the bundle's pipeline script, which is the plain-Python equivalent of the Nextflow description: for every participant directory it runs the validation script against the public reference dataset, then the metrics script against the gold-standard directory, and finally the consolidation script, which writes a data model export and a leaderboard image. One detail to watch, read from the splitting document rather than the README: the cross-validation scripts read cv_fold_assignment.csv, which is Strategy 1, kept for backward compatibility, so using the recommended Strategy 3 locally means pointing the gold-standard directory at a copy of the Strategy 3 fold file under that name.

> **Original work.** The benchmark was published by Schweke H, Xu Q, Tauriello G, *et al.* (2023) *Discriminating physiological from non-physiological interfaces in structures of protein complexes: A community-wide study.* Proteomics 23(17):e2200323, [doi:10.1002/pmic.202200323](https://doi.org/10.1002/pmic.202200323). The data come from the community repository [vibbits/Elixir-3DBioInfo-Benchmark-Protein-Interfaces](https://github.com/vibbits/Elixir-3DBioInfo-Benchmark-Protein-Interfaces). This repository turns the benchmark into an OpenEBench experiment

OpenEBench implementation of the ELIXIR 3D-BioInfo benchmark for discriminating physiological from crystallographic (non-physiological) protein homodimer interfaces: schema-validated OpenEBench metadata (Community, Benchmarking Event, Challenge, Metrics, Tools, Contacts), the datasets of 14 reference scoring methods (13 research groups and a random-forest consensus), the gold-standard labels, four homology-aware cross-validation fold assignments, the benchmark workflow scripts (validation, metric computation, consolidation), and a static web page that evaluates new predictions in the browser and ranks them against the reference methods.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Either, and the package distinguishes them. Thirteen of the reference methods are single fixed scores used as submitted, while the random-forest consensus is a trained classifier whose leave-one-out probabilities are used unchanged and are not retrained within the folds. A new submission is a score file, so a method may be trained however its authors wish; what the folds control is the threshold fitting, which in the published table happens on training folds only.

quotes.text: **Random-forest consensus.** Unlike the other 13 methods, which are single fixed scores, the consensus is a trained classifier. Its scores are the leave-one-out probabilities provided in the original benchmark repository (`random_forest_analysis/rf_topk221.out`), used unchanged and not retrained within the folds above. Leave-one-out does not remove homologous entries from the training set, so its AUROC should be read as an upper estimate with respect to the other methods.

strengths.text: The splits are designed against the leakage this dataset actually has, with the figure stated: 60 per cent of entries share a CATH superfamily with another entry, so homologous interfaces are kept in one fold, and no group spans folds in any of the four strategies.

quotes.text: 1000 of 1671 benchmark entries (60%) share a CATH superfamily with at least one other entry. A random split would routinely place near-identical or homologous interfaces in both the training and held-out folds of the same run, inflating any cross-validated performance estimate.
All four give exactly zero groups spanning more than one fold (verified).

strengths.text: The package says what it did and did not inherit: the folds are its own proposal and explicitly not the folds of the original study, and the reference scores are the ones the groups submitted to the original repository.

quotes.text: **These splits are defined for this package; they are not the folds of Schweke et al.** (Strategies 1 and 3 are grouping rules defined for this package, Strategy 2 is a clustering computed for this package with MMseqs2, and Strategy 2b is the BLASTClust clustering of this benchmark, published in `data/ppi_benchmark_seqs.clust_25_05`.) The manuscript describes a 5-fold cross-validated ROC analysis used to select the best score of each group and its threshold (the point of the ROC most distant from the diagonal; Methods 2.3 and Figure S1 of the supplement). The folds of that analysis are not reproduced here. The splits below keep homologous interfaces together in one fold, and are a proposal of this package.
The scores of the 13 research groups are those submitted to the original benchmark repository; the random-forest consensus uses the leave-one-out probabilities provided there.

strengths.text: The two caveats a reader needs are printed next to the table rather than buried: that the consensus row is a trained classifier whose AUROC is an upper estimate, and that methods scored between 1,123 and 1,671 entries so rows are not strictly comparable.

quotes.text: Benchmark task: discriminate **physiological** from **crystallographic (non-physiological)** protein homodimer interfaces. 1,671 curated entries (840 physiological, 831 non-physiological).

## Strategy 3 -- Combined union of Strategy 1 + Strategy 2b (RECOMMENDED) Two entries are forced into the same fold if EITHER signal links them: same CATH superfamily/gene (Strategy 1) OR same blastclust sequence cluster (Strategy 2b), computed as connected components of the union graph. This is the most conservative option against leakage (a structural match some sequence-clustering misses due to low sequence identity at a conserved fold, or vice versa, is still caught), at the cost of coarser groups (688 components, largest 132 entries)

steps.title: Put the predictions where the pipeline looks for them
steps.explanation: The pipeline script loops over every directory under datasets/participant and reads predictions.csv inside it, so a new method is added by creating a directory with that file. The two commands are written here from what the script reads; the sources give the path, not a command.

quotes.text: # Runs the full validate -> metrics -> consolidate pipeline for every participant # in datasets/participant/*, then consolidates into one leaderboard.

python3 "$HERE/workflow/validate.py" \ --input "$pdir/predictions.csv" \ --public_ref_dir "$HERE/datasets/public_reference" \ --community_id OEBC_3DBioinfo --challenges_ids 3DBioinfo:PPI-PhysioClassification \ --participant_id "$pid" --outdir "$OUTDIR/validation_out/$pid" || true

steps.title: Run validation, scoring and consolidation
steps.explanation: This is the bundle's own local pipeline, described in the script as the plain-Python equivalent of the Nextflow skeleton. It runs validate.py against the public reference directory, then compute_metrics.py against the metrics reference directory, for each participant, and finally consolidate.py for the leaderboard. An output directory can be passed as the first argument; it defaults to a directory beside the repository root.

quotes.text: # Runs the full validate -> metrics -> consolidate pipeline for every participant # in datasets/participant/*, then consolidates into one leaderboard.

python3 "$HERE/workflow/consolidate.py" \ --assess_dir "$OUTDIR/assessment_out" --community_id OEBC_3DBioinfo \ --challenge_id 3DBioinfo:PPI-PhysioClassification --outdir "$OUTDIR/consolidated" echo "Done. See $OUTDIR/consolidated/data_model_export.json and leaderboard.svg"

notes: Numbers and names worth a reviewer's eye. The 1,671 entries are the curated annotation's 1,677 less six flagged for deletion, and the Zenodo record states this annotation differs for 16 entries from the original 2023 publication, which had 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological against 840 and 831 here. The n column of the reference table is not the benchmark size: methods scored between 1,123 and 1,671 entries and each is evaluated on its own subset, so the structured size records the benchmark's 1,671 and the size unit records that range. The structured split is Strategy 3 because that is what the published table and the page's default recommendation use; the repository's own cross-validation scripts read the Strategy 1 fold file for backward compatibility, which a local reproduction has to change deliberately. Two inconsistencies were found by reading the code: the README asks a submitter for columns entry_id and score while workflow/validate.py requires entry_id and raw_score, and compute_metrics.py derives its decision threshold from the scored population by Youden's J whenever no published threshold is passed, flagging it as data-driven. The Zenodo record for this version says 1.0.0 while the README's citation block says 1.2.0 for the concept DOI. The released date is the Zenodo publication date of this version, not a last-modified timestamp. Everything in the package is CC BY-NC 4.0, so no repository bytes are stored; the Zenodo API response is stored as the brief allows.
